articles.title: For New York’s Haitian community, annual West Indian Day Parade means more in trying times
articles.summary: Steel drums, flag-draped floats, and the smell of jerk chicken will fill Brooklyn’s Eastern Parkway on Monday, as hundreds of thousands turn out for the West Indian Day Parade.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Steel drums, flag-draped floats, and the smell of jerk chicken will fill Brooklyn’s Eastern Parkway on Monday, as hundreds of thousands turn out for the West Indian Day Parade, one of the largest celebrations of Caribbean culture in the country. This year, Haitians are marching under more solemn circumstances than in prior years. Federal immigration enforcement has intensified against Caribbean and other Black immigrant communities over the past year, and Haitians have lost a key protection — temporary protected status. Known as TPS, it let hundreds of thousands remain in the U.S. legally. Organizers say the parade has become both a defiant assertion of pride and a rare bright spot in a traumatic year. “There’s a somber cloud over it with everything that has happened from last year to this year with TPS ... what’s happening in detention centers, and those who are being sent back with no valid way of living or supporting themselves,” said Natalie Lafontant, a Brooklyn native who organizes Lespri Ayiti, or “Spirit of Haiti,” the largest Haitian “mas” — short for masquerade — or marching community in Monday’s parade. Still, she said, the response to hardship is not surrender. “But if you know anything about the Caribbean, especially about Haiti, we use music, dance, art, to continue to strive and push through,” Lafontant said while taking stock of parade costumes at a community center. Keeping parade plans alive amid anti-immigrant policies In June, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Mullin v. Doe that federal courts cannot review the Trump administration’s decision to end temporary protected status for Haitian and Syrian immigrants, clearing the way for roughly 350,000 Haitians to lose the protection. A federal judge finalized the order in early August, and work permits tied to Haitian TPS expired July 27. Lafontant’s group, comprising about 180 artists, designers, musicians and residents, is marching in the parade for the second year. The group struggled to find float sponsors this year. “All the insurances that we’ve got to cover, the people who walk, you’ve got to take care of them, the costumes, the designers. You add that all up, it’s a very hefty bill. But we continue to do it because we love our country,” said Lafontant. Haitians’ history with New York goes back decades Lafontant is part of a Haitian community that numbers roughly 163,000 in the New York metropolitan area, according to the Migration Policy Institute — the second-largest Haitian population in the U.S. after the Miami metropolitan area. Most Haitian migrants settled in Brooklyn neighborhoods including Flatbush, East Flatbush and Crown Heights. Haitians arrived in New York in waves beginning under the dictatorship of Jean-Claude “Baby Doc” Duvalier, whose regime’s repression and economic collapse drove many to leave the island in the 1970s and 1980s. The migration continued after his 1986 ouster. Haiti’s history of resistance runs deeper still, back to the Haitian Revolution, when enslaved and free Black people overthrew French colonial rule in what is widely regarded as the only successful slave revolt in modern history, culminating in the 1803 Battle of Vertières. The victory paved the way for Haiti’s independence the following year. That history of resistance remains a source of pride for Haitians far beyond the country’s shores, even among generations who have built new lives abroad. Edwina Paul, founder of SPM, or “Fanm Se Poto Mitan” — “Women Are the Pillar of Society” — left Haiti in 1993 to start a new life with her husband in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Canarsie. Paul, whose coalition of Haitian women leaders and organizers is marching Monday, said conditions in Haiti are what pushed people to leave. “It’s not safe there. Coming here is like an umbrella for us to be safe from that,” she said of those fleeing the country’s gang violence and instability. “We don’t come here to sin, we don’t come here to kill. We come here to work, to have a better education.” Anticipation for electrifying lineup of Haitian pop, fashion SPM’s resilience is stitched into its costumes this year. Clara Poteau, a fashion designer and an alumna of the Fashion Institute of Technology, designed royal blue emperor robes in the image of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, a lieutenant and leader of the Haitian Revolution and the first leader of an independent Haiti. A total of six designers and one painter spent a month hand-painting costumes that commemorate Haitian achievements, working through the weekend before the parade: dresses covered in miniature Haitian flags, skirts bearing the faces of Duckens Nazon and Emmanuel Sanon, the national football players who hold Haiti’s international scoring records, at 44 and 47 goals, respectively. One orange T-shirt, dubbed the “Freedom” tee, carries the flags of nations Haitian revolutionary leaders helped liberate with shelter, money, weapons, and troops, including Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Panama, Mexico and Greece. The sound of the mas, the first taste of Haitian energy parade attendees will experience before seeing the group, is carried forward by Jesus Luc, a Harlem native and Lespri Ayiti’s band manager. Luc coordinated a lineup built around “Raboday,” a popular genre of contemporary Haitian and Caribbean sounds, and Kompa, Haiti’s signature native dance music. Headlining is DJ Comix of the band Team Madada, dubbed by Luc as “probably the most popular group in Haiti,” part of a new generation of sound defining the country’s youth. “It’s electrifying. It’s music that will touch your soul. Between the music and the costumes... it’s the heart of the people that’s going to be there.”

articles.title: North Korea and Russia open their first road bridge, state media reports
articles.summary: North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge on Monday, Russia’s TASS state news agency reported.
articles.body: MOSCOW — North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge on Monday, Russia’s TASS state news agency reported, a structure which spans the Tumen river and which both sides cast as an important milestone in their strategic partnership. The bridge is located near the existing “Friendship Bridge”, a rail bridge which was commissioned in 1959 after the Korean war. There are already direct air and rail links between Moscow and Pyongyang. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the bridge should spur development between the two countries in various spheres — including tourism — and create new jobs. “I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” TASS cited Mishustin as saying at the bridge’s opening ceremony via video link. Construction of the new bridge, which had been under discussion for years, began in April last year after its construction was agreed during a visit by President Vladimir Putin to North Korea in 2024. The two countries’ ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022 with Pyongyang sending thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help repel a 2024 Ukrainian incursion there.

articles.title: Body of war criminal Mladic lies in state in Serbian capital ahead of funeral
articles.summary: The body of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb commander who died while serving a life sentence for war crimes, lay in state on Monday as Serbia defied European Union warnings against allowing public homage to the man found guilty of the continent’s first case of genocide since World War II.
articles.body: The body of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb commander who died while serving a life sentence for war crimes, lay in state on Monday as Serbia defied European Union warnings against allowing public homage to the man found guilty of the continent’s first case of genocide since World War II. Thousands of mourners arrived early at the small Serbian Orthodox Church of St. Luke in Belgrade to honor Mladic, who is still viewed as a hero by many Serbs. His military officer’s cap and saber rested on the coffin, which was flanked by men in fatigues. Pro-government media in Serbia reported that Mladic will receive full military honors while the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, will lead the funeral service. Mladic “was a man who gave everything in his life for the Serbian people,” said Milan Dobric, a mourner who traveled from Kosovo for the funeral. “I am glad that this morning people are coming to pay special respect.” Mladic died at 84 on Aug. 27 in The Hague, Netherlands, while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity his troops committed during the Bosnian war in 1992-95. While the funeral arrangements were formally made by Mladic’s family, the Serbian government sent a plane last week to bring his remains to Belgrade, and soldiers carried his coffin wrapped in the national flag. A military commemoration was held Saturday at an official Serbian army venue. Populist President Aleksandar Vucic, a former extreme nationalist who supported Serbia’s expansionist policies during the war, described the funeral as an “emotional outpouring” that “has nothing to do with whether Vucic allowed something or not.” Serbia is a candidate nation for European Union membership and has faced strong criticism for honoring Mladic after his death. Marta Kos, the enlargement commissioner for the bloc, canceled an upcoming visit to Serbia in protest, arguing that “the glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.” Serbia, which backed Bosnian Serb forces during the war, remains defiant over its wartime role and accuses the West of anti-Serb bias. Vucic said that “we (Serbs) have been persecuted and harassed for 30, 40 years .. always guilty whatever happens,” He added that “people just won’t take it any more.” Vucic, who is not attending the funeral, previously has accused Kos of “lying.” The Serbian president has stepped up his anti-Western rhetoric ahead of an early parliamentary election expected next month. A number of other European officials joined the criticism of Serbia, along with regional leaders and relatives of Mladic’s victims from the war in Bosnia. The conflict left more than 100,000 people dead and over 1 million homeless before it ended in 1995 in a U.S.-brokered peace agreement. Mladic was sentenced in 2017 for orchestrating the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslims in Srebrenica in 1995; the yearslong siege of the Bosnian capital of Sarajevo and other war crimes, including setting up concentration camps for detained non-Serb civilians and enemy soldiers. Since Mladic died, his nationalist admirers have held vigils, painted a series of murals with his image in Belgrade and lit flares in his honor. On Sunday evening, soccer fans displayed a huge image of Mladic and chanted his name at a match in Belgrade. Serbia has refused to recognize that genocide was committed in Srebrenica, calling the massacre a “horrific crime” instead. Last year, Serbia buried another convicted war criminal, the former army chief of staff Nebojsa Pavkovic, with full military honors at a cemetery for distinguished individuals. The Balkan nation’s EU bid has stalled due to democratic backsliding and Vucic’s refusal to join international sanctions against Russia over the invasion of Ukraine. A U.N. “safe haven” for Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims), Srebrenica ended up being overrun by Serbs who forced men and boys to strip, killed them and bulldozed their bodies into mass graves. The war started after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia when ethnic Serbs in Bosnia took control over swaths of Bosnian territory to form a country of their own and unite it with Serbia.

articles.title: At least 11 killed after avalanche hits climbers in Russia’s North Caucasus
articles.summary: At least 11 people were killed and six ​others injured after an avalanche ‌struck a group of climbers in Russia’s Kabardino-Balkaria region in the ​North Caucasus, local emergency ​services said.
articles.body: At least 11 people were killed and six ​others injured after an avalanche ‌struck a group of climbers in Russia’s Kabardino-Balkaria region in the ​North Caucasus, local emergency ​services said. The avalanche swept down ⁠Mount Mizhirgi, one of the ​highest peaks in Russia’s North ​Caucasus, at around 5 p.m. local time (9 a.m. EST) on Sunday, hitting a ​group of 33 climbers. As of ​9 a.m. local time on Monday, 10 ‌climbers ⁠had made their own way down the mountain, while the fate of six others ​remained unknown, ​emergency ⁠services said. More than 50 emergency workers were involved ​in the search and ​rescue ⁠operation, but efforts were being hampered by difficult terrain and ⁠a ​high risk of ​further avalanches, they said.

articles.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ makes it 6 weeks in a row at No. 1 as Hollywood wraps a banner summer
articles.summary: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” remained the No. 1 movie in theaters over the weekend, becoming just the second film this decade to top the box office for six straight weeks.
articles.body: NEW YORK — “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” remained the No. 1 movie in theaters over the weekend, becoming just the second film this decade to top the box office for six straight weeks. Since the end of July, the Sony superhero movie has ruled over cinemas with rare dominance. The last release to enjoy such a long stretch leading the box office was 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water.” “Brand New Day,” the fourth standalone Spider-Man film starring Tom Holland, collected $18 million over the weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday. Sony is forecasting $23.3 million for the four-day holiday weekend. “Brand New Day” has grossed $2.4 billion worldwide. Universal Pictures’ “The Odyssey,” as it has for much of the “Spider-Man” run, remained in second place. Christopher Nolan’s epic added $13 million domestically over the weekend, bringing its global haul to $1.63 billion. More than $1 billion of that has come from overseas sales, making “The Odyssey” the first to achieve that international milestone since 2009’s “Avatar.” Both blockbusters — “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” — helped lead Hollywood to its best summer since before the pandemic. Through Aug. 31, the domestic box office totaled $4.6 billion for the season, according to Rentrak, an increase of 26.1% from 2025 and just shy of 2013’s record summer. On Sunday, Rentrak forecast that, including the Labor Day weekend, the summer will end up with $4.759 billion, a whisker above the $4.758 billion of summer 2013. That time frame, though, spans 130 days this year, compared with 123 days in 2013. Accounting for inflation and higher ticket prices, Hollywood’s summer wasn’t quite so historically sensational. Admissions are still well below pre-pandemic marks. But it’s nevertheless a remarkable rebound for a film industry that has struggled to string together such a hit-filled summer through the pandemic, labor strife and the expansion of streaming. Labor Day weekend is typically a sleepy time in theaters. And neither new release — Paramount’s “By Any Means” and A24’s “Onslaught” — made much of a mark. One of the weekend’s best performers was “Coyote vs. Acme,” the hybrid live-action-animated Looney Tunes movie. It dipped a modest 29% to gross $11.3 million in its second weekend. “Coyote vs. Acme” is turning out to be a good investment for Ketchup Entertainment. The indie distributor acquired the film for approximately $50 million after Warner Bros., which produced the $70 million film, opted to can it. In two weeks, “Coyote vs. Acme” has ridden strong reviews and good word-of-mouth to $33.8 million domestically. “By Any Means,” a 1960s-set civil rights action thriller starring Mark Wahlberg and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, opened with $7.4 million. Paramount is projecting $9.2 million for the four-day holiday weekend. Audiences gave it a “B+” CinemaScore. “Onslaught,” however, flopped with $1.9 million on 1,918 screens for the three-day weekend and a projection of $2.3 million for the four-day weekend. The A24 release, directed by Adam Wingard, stars Adria Arjona as a former Army sniper who defends her trailer park home from three escaped, experimental super soldiers. “Onslaught” cost a modest $15 million to make. But reviews (57% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes) and audience scores (a “C” CinemaScore) weren’t good. Meanwhile, “Buddy,” a low-budget dark comedy, has turned into a surprise success. Made for just $3 million, the film, directed by Casper Kelly and from the producers of “Weapons,” is about a group of children trapped inside a surreal 1990s children’s television series. After overperforming in its opening weekend, “Buddy” actually increased its ticket sales over its second weekend. The film grossed $5.7 million, up 5%, to bring its two-week total to $14.3 million. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $18 million. 2. “The Odyssey,” $13 million. 3. “Coyote vs. Acme,” $11.3 million. 4. “By Any Means,” $7.4 million. 5. “Insidious: Out of the Further,” $6.5 million. 6. “Cars” (20th anniversary): $6.1 million. 7. “Buddy,” $5.7 million. 8. “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie,” $3.3 million. 9. “The End of Oak Street,” $2.9 million. 10. “The Dog Stars,” $2.7 million.

articles.title: U.K. government condemns anti-immigrant demonstrators at port city
articles.summary: Britain’s government condemned hundreds of protesters who blocked streets in the English coastal city of Portsmouth to try to stop the arrival of migrants from France.
articles.body: LONDON — The British government on Monday condemned the “intimidating and thuggish behavior” of anti-immigrant demonstrators who converged on a port in southern England where migrants were brought ashore after crossing the English Channel. Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in dark clothing and wearing masks, faced off with police in Portsmouth late Sunday in an attempt to prevent lifeboats from bringing the migrants to land. They then tried to block buses carrying the new arrivals to a processing facility for asylum seekers. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder,” the government said in a statement. The Portsmouth protest came a day after hundreds of masked anti-immigration protesters blocked roads leading to Britain’s busiest ferry port of Dover on Saturday, clogging traffic and disrupting travelers as well as cargo vehicles heading for France. Both groups appeared to be led by Daniel Thomas, an ally of veteran far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, better known as Tommy Robinson. Successive U.K. governments have struggled to stop people — more than 40,000 last year — making the dangerous journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians including Nigel Farage of the hard-right party Reform UK, and has been used as a rallying point by anti-immigration activists. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government says stepped-up law enforcement cooperation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40% compared with 2025. The boat carrying about 140 people to Portsmouth had left early Sunday from Normandy, far west of the beaches near Calais where most departures have taken place — making it a much longer and riskier journey. Britain’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said lifeboats, a coastguard helicopter and a plane were involved in the operation to bring the migrants to shore.

articles.title: Satya Niketan building collapse puts Delhi’s ageing real estate stock under scrutiny
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Delhi government on Monday said it was working with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) to make periodic structural audits and saf.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi government on Monday said it was working with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) to make periodic structural audits and safety certifications mandatory for buildings used for public activities. Structures include paying guest (PG) accommodations, nursing homes and schools, following the collapse of a building in Satya Niketan that killed six people.Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta announced the proposed policy during her visit to the Satya Niketan site, where rescue and debris-clearing operations continued. The move is expected to put greater scrutiny on ageing buildings that have been converted or adapted for high-occupancy uses, particularly PGs and other properties where structural alterations can increase safety risks."The government, in collaboration with the Municipal Corporation, is formulating a policy mandating that any building intended for public use—whether a PG, nursing home, school, or any other facility—must undergo periodic structural audits and safety certifications; otherwise, no public activity will be permitted there."The proposed framework could significantly tighten compliance requirements for Delhi's ageing building stock, particularly properties operating as student housing and other accommodation facilities. Buildings failing to obtain the required safety certification would not be allowed to continue public-facing activities under the proposed policy.Gupta also said the government would not permit residents to remain in buildings considered unsafe and said alternative accommodation had been arranged for people evacuated from the collapsed property."We will not allow anyone to reside in unsafe PGs. We have arranged accommodation in college hostels for those evacuated from the building, and the government is ensuring their needs are met. We are in contact with the parents of the students affected by this tragedy and are providing them with full support to alleviate their distress. Regarding government officials whose oversight, negligence, or other lapses contributed to this situation, strict action will be taken against them this very day; no one will be spared," she added.Basement work under scrutinyThe collapse has also brought the structural condition and subsequent alterations of the property under scrutiny. Delhi minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said preliminary information indicated that the building was around 40 to 50 years old and that work in its basement may have triggered the collapse."The information received so far indicates that while this building was 40-50 years old, attempts were made to carry out work in its basement, which triggered this accident. The Chief Minister stated yesterday itself that strict action would be taken regarding the issues raised," he told reporters.The episode highlights a key challenge for Delhi's real estate landscape: older buildings being used for purposes that may involve substantially different occupancy levels and structural demands from those for which they were originally designed. The government's proposed audit regime could therefore bring building age, structural modifications and safety certification into sharper focus for property owners and operators.An adjoining structure at the site, also estimated to be 40 to 50 years old, has already been evacuated and is slated for demolition. However, authorities said it cannot be brought down immediately because the structure is unstable and the condition beneath the debris remains uncertain."The NDRF team is continuously engaged in the operation. You can see that this situation involves a high degree of sensitivity because the building visible in the background is also 40–50 years old. It poses a major challenge for the NDRF to ensure no damage occurs to the adjacent building while clearing the debris from below and checking for any further casualties. However, the NDRF is a highly capable force; I have gathered information and spoken with the NDRF chief. The adjacent building will definitely be demolished—it has already been evacuated and is slated for demolition. But the challenge right now is that the structure is currently unstable; we do not yet know the condition beneath the accumulated debris, so it cannot be demolished immediately," he said.MCD orders demolitionThe MCD had on Sunday ordered the demolition of the collapsed building at Property No. 13, Satya Niketan, within three days, describing it as being in a "ruinous/dangerous condition" and warning that it posed a risk to occupants as well as people in the surrounding neighbourhood.Gupta returned to the site on Monday and met National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) officials to review the ongoing search, rescue and debris-removal operation. The operation remains underway.The collapse has also triggered protests over building safety and administrative accountability. The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) and the National Students' Union of India (NSUI) demonstrated on Monday, demanding action against those responsible.NSUI president Vinod Jakhar alleged that the rescue response exposed wider shortcomings in disaster preparedness, including a lack of planning, equipment, management and an adequate rescue team.With the death toll at six and the search operation still continuing, the Satya Niketan incident has put renewed focus on the safety of Delhi's ageing properties, particularly those being used as high-density residential or public facilities. The proposed mandatory certification policy could mark a significant shift towards periodic structural scrutiny rather than relying primarily on action after buildings are declared dangerous or suffer structural failures.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Bakery can't make handmade empanadas fast enough as tourists descend on nation's oldest city
articles.summary: Baked empanadas at the Spanish Bakery & Cafe have drawn crowds since 1965, connecting St. Augustine visitors to the city's deep Spanish roots.
articles.body: At the Spanish Bakery & Café in St. Augustine, Florida, a tray of 16 empanadas doesn't necessarily last long. On a busy day, bakery manager Carol Miller said customers can scoop them up as soon as they're made. "There are times when we'll sell through three trays within an hour, not even," Miller told Fox News Digital. "So, it really depends. There is a lot of craze for these empanadas, and they do go very fast." The attention may be fueled by tourists, recommendations and social media, but the bakery's empanadas are hardly a new addition to St. Augustine's food scene. Miller said they date to the bakery's opening in 1965. CENTURY-OLD ITALIAN ICE RECIPE IS CREATING CHILDHOOD MEMORIES FOR A WHOLE NEW GENERATION "We actually make everything from hand ourselves – the doughs, the mixes, pressing them, everything," she said. Making enough to satisfy the crowds takes work. Producing 10 trays using the bakery's former hand-rolling process could consume an eight-hour shift, Miller said. A newer rolling machine has cut that time to about four hours. With 16 empanadas to a tray, that's 160 at a time. While plenty of customers happen upon the bakery while exploring St. Augustine, others arrive knowing exactly what they want. Miller said visitors mention everything from news coverage to TikTok and Instagram posts as reasons for stopping by to try the empanadas for themselves. AMERICANS ARE PAYING PEOPLE TO WAIT IN LINE FOR TIKTOK-FAMOUS FOOD The bakery also draws on its surroundings. Located in St. Augustine's historic district, it offers visitors a connection to the city's Spanish identity. "I think because we are mainly Spanish culture in the colonial quarter here, it is nice that we go back to our Spanish roots here specifically," Miller said. "On top of that, we are a healthier version since we are baked instead of the traditional fried." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER That distinction is particularly appealing in Florida's warmer months, Miller said, when visitors spending the day walking around town or heading to the beach may be looking for something hearty without choosing another fried option. For people hesitant to order an empanada, customers sometimes incorrectly assume the filling will be spicy simply because it's Spanish cuisine, Miller said. The bakery, she said, tries to make its food welcoming to the broad mix of people who visit St. Augustine. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Not everyone, however, visits because of the hype. Alexis Rapchak, a 12-year-old visiting from Ohio on her first trip to St. Augustine, was trying one of the empanadas for the first time. Asked how she'd heard about the bakery, her answer was simple: "I didn't. I just showed up." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ But she described it as "really good." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I really like the dough and the inside," she said. "It's perfect."

articles.title: A Massachusetts group restored 44 acres of wetland and a mile of stream; butterflies soon appeared that locals had never seen there
articles.summary: US News: A former cranberry-growing landscape in Harwich, Massachusetts, is showing what can happen when a damaged wetland is given the chance to function natu.
articles.body: A former cranberry-growing landscape in Harwich, Massachusetts, is showing what can happen when a damaged wetland is given the chance to function naturally again. The Harwich Conservation Trust (HCT) spent years working with public agencies and other partners to restore the Robert F. Smith Cold Brook Preserve, a 66-acre property in the heart of Harwich Port. Completed in 2025, the project rewilded more than 44 acres of wetland and nearly a mile of stream, while creating ponds, restoring native vegetation and improving water flow. Then came an unexpected sign that the landscape was changing. As the restoration work neared completion, longtime HCT volunteer Gerry Beetham began noticing butterflies he had not seen there before, including common buckeyes and clouded sulphurs. The return of these insects offered a small but vivid glimpse of a much larger ecological recovery.A former cranberry bog was transformed into a wildlife oasisFor more than a century, Cold Brook had been shaped around cranberry farming, leaving the stream and surrounding wetlands significantly altered from their natural condition. The land eventually became a retired cranberry bog, and in 2001, the Trust acquired the property. Years of planning followed before the restoration could begin. The project was designed to bring back more natural wetland and stream functions while improving habitat for wildlife. Work included reshaping Cold Brook into a more natural, winding channel, creating four ponds of different sizes, adding a salt marsh and planting native trees and shrubs. Old water-control structures that had interfered with the flow were also addressed. By 2025, the restored stream could once again move freely through the preserve for the first time in more than a century, reconnecting the landscape with the wider watershed towards Saquatucket Harbour.The 44-acre restoration changed more than the landscapeThe restoration was not simply about making Cold Brook look more natural. The aim was to rebuild the ecological functions that had been disrupted by decades of agricultural use. More than 44 acres of adjacent wetland habitat were rewilded, while nearly a mile of stream was restored. The design incorporated ponds, native plantings and a more varied landscape intended to create different habitats for wildlife. HCT says the work has already produced benefits including greater habitat diversity, improved water quality and stronger stormwater absorption by the recovering wetlands. Restoring the stream also improved fish passage, while the wetlands gained greater resilience in the face of a changing climate. A half-mile wheelchair-accessible All Persons Trail was added as part of the wider project, meaning the ecological transformation also created a new way for people of different ages and abilities to experience the recovering landscape.Butterflies appeared as native plants returned to Cold BrookOne of the most visible signs of the transformation came from an animal small enough to be easily overlooked. As the restoration was nearing completion, HCT volunteer Gerry Beetham noticed butterflies at Cold Brook that he had not previously seen there. Among them were common buckeyes and clouded sulphurs. For Beetham, their arrival was evidence that the newly restored landscape was beginning to provide the resources butterflies need, from nectar-producing flowers to plants where they can lay eggs and their caterpillars can develop. HCT had already planted a pollinator garden at the preserve in 2025, creating additional habitat for vulnerable butterflies such as monarchs, swallowtails and skippers. Monarchs have since become frequent visitors. The change is a reminder that ecological restoration can produce effects that are visible far beyond the original stream and wetland project.Cold Brook has become a living test of ecological recoveryThe butterfly sightings are now part of a much broader story unfolding at the preserve. HCT is using Cold Brook not only as a restored natural area but also as a place where people can observe how ecosystems respond when natural processes are allowed to return. The organisation is participating in Butterfly Big Day 2026, with a field class scheduled for September 12 where participants can identify butterflies and learn how native plants support pollinators. Observations from the event will be submitted to iNaturalist as part of an international effort involving organisations across several countries. HCT is also preparing a Cape Cod BioBlitz at Cold Brook, where volunteers will document as many species as possible. Together, these activities turn the preserve into something more than a scenic trail, they provide an opportunity to track biodiversity as a restored wetland continues to develop.The transformation of Cold Brook shows why restoration can be measured in more than acres of land or miles of stream. A landscape that once revolved around commercial cranberry production is now supporting native plants, wetlands, flowing water and an expanding range of wildlife. The butterflies noticed by Beetham may seem like a modest detail beside the scale of the engineering and conservation work, but they offer an immediate sign that the changes are reaching living species. HCT says Cold Brook now functions as a wildlife oasis, with ecological benefits already appearing across the preserve. The project was funded and supported through a partnership involving HCT donors, Town of Harwich voters, the Harwich Community Preservation Fund, the Massachusetts Division of Ecological Restoration, MassTrails and the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kenya minister warns foreigners against 'misusing' visas to trade
articles.summary: Kenya is due to start enforcing measures to restrict foreign nationals from operating small-scale businesses.
articles.body:
Kenya's trade ministry has warned foreign nationals that visa-free entry into the country does not grant them the right to work, as the government vows to shut down unlicensed small businesses run by foreigners.

President William Ruto had set today as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work.

Ahead of the move, the Burundian embassy in Kenya said it would offer emergency free travel documents to its citizens willing to go back home, amid reports of the mistreatment of Burundians.

It is unclear how many foreign nationals are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.

In a statement, the trade ministry said there was a "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", adding that some entered Kenya as investors or tourists but then got involved in business activities in breach of their declared status.

"Owing to the high number of foreigners involved in the retail and local trade sectors, there is therefore a need to align their activities and ensure compliance with work permit provisions," Trade Minister Lee Kinyanjui said.

Last week, Ruto said that Kenya remained open to foreign investment, but it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".

He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.

Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.

Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".

"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.

Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.

Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi.

Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.

On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities.

"Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.

The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.

Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.

He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.

"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."

Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.

Additional reporting by Akisa Wandera and Prime Ndikumagenge

articles.title: I'm the acting secretary of Labor and I'm here to say thank you to the American worker
articles.summary: Trump's acting secretary of Labor highlights manufacturing growth, apprenticeships and AI job training in a Labor Day tribute to American workers.
articles.body: For 250 years, American workers have shown the world time and again that they are the best. From the transcontinental railroad, the skyscrapers of New York City, the arsenal of democracy that won two world wars, and the tech revolution of the last several decades, every stage of American ingenuity and innovation was made possible because we trusted the hard-working men and women of this country to do what they do best: Build, create, and innovate, and leave a legacy that their children can be proud of. LIZ PEEK: THE TRUMP ECONOMY IS DOING BETTER THAN THE MEDIA WANT TO ADMIT So, this Labor Day, as President Donald Trump’s acting secretary of Labor, I want to say thank you. Thank you for building the homes that we raise our families in. Thank you for building factories that showed the world the power of industry. Thank you for building the highways and railroads that tied our communities together. And thank you for your hard work and perseverance, even as successive generations of governments took you for granted. Under President Trump’s leadership, I can assure you those days are over. Today, the American worker is at the center of our nation’s economic agenda and of our industrial revival, because every American should be able to work, raise their children and worship God in the communities that their parents and grandparents built for them. BESSENT CREDITS TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICIES WITH HELPING RETURN JOBS TO AMERICANS AS WAGE GAINS RESUME Last month the economy added 162,000 jobs, and we’ve created more than 1 million private sector jobs since President Trump took office. Instead of leaving factories to rot and rust, we are revitalizing communities by building new ones and heralding a new era of American industrial might. After years of decline, American manufacturing has expanded for eight straight months. The jobs that were lost overseas are coming back and renewing the communities that were left behind, the economy is growing, paychecks are getting bigger, and more Americans are working than at any point in our nation’s history. But more importantly, we’re sowing the seeds of a historic economic boom. President Trump has secured trillions of dollars in new investments from companies and countries alike. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM Manufacturing and construction jobs have grown for three straight months. And we’ve expanded opportunities in the skilled trades through registered apprenticeships, to ensure American workers can find dignified and high-paying careers wherever they choose to live. Instead of treating the advent of artificial intelligence as an inevitable source of job loss, we are developing training programs for AI integration so that this revolutionary technology becomes a source of job creation, business expansion and wage growth. JENSEN HUANG SAYS AI WILL RESHAPE WORK LIKE THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION AND THE US 'SHOULD ABSOLUTELY LEAD' American workers once built the rockets that took us to the moon and made advancements in energy production that our ancestors could only dream of. Today, the American worker is taking the world to Mars, achieving lifesaving advances in medicine and exploring the very limits of human potential. All because some brilliant and hard-working Americans dedicate themselves to a mission and see it to completion. At universities across the country there is an army of young Americans working in the STEM fields ready to take on the tech jobs of the future. And in towns and cities across America, there are millions of young Americans who are eager to help build things and feel a rush of pride when they see the sticker that says, "Made in America." TRUMP TAPS ACTING LABOR SECRETARY KEITH SONDERLING FOR PERMANENT ROLE PENDING SENATE CONFIRMATION The greatest privilege of my job as Acting Secretary of Labor is getting to see up close how Americans from Texas to Ohio, to Florida, New Mexico and beyond, are showing the world that we are a hardworking, devoted, patriotic and innovative people. So this Labor Day, I hope all American workers take a moment to pause and reflect on the important work you do for our country. At President Trump’s Department of Labor we are using Labor Day as an opportunity to recommit ourselves to ensuring that the American worker remains our nation’s greatest asset and that we are there for them every single day. articles.title: Defence ministry clears Rs 1.10 lakh crore acquisition proposals for Army, Navy, Air Force
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) on Monday approved the in-principle administrative clearance, or Acceptance of Necessity (AoN), for d.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) on Monday approved the in-principle administrative clearance, or Acceptance of Necessity (AoN), for defence acquisition proposals worth around Rs 1.10 lakh crore.The approvals cover requirements of the Indian Army, Navy and Air Force, with about 98% of the procurements expected to be sourced from Indian industry, according to the defence ministry.Defence minister Rajnath Singh chaired the DAC meeting on September 7. Army to get CBRN vehicles, helicopters and bridging systemsFor the Army, the DAC cleared proposals for Chemical Biological Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) reconnaissance vehicles, High Mobility Vehicles, Self-Propelled Mechanical Mine Layers, Advanced Light Helicopters, Trawl Tanks and the Sarvatra Bridge System.The CBRN reconnaissance vehicles will be used to detect, identify, monitor and mark areas contaminated by CBRN agents.The High Mobility Vehicles are intended to support operational and logistical requirements and improve mobility in difficult terrain. The mine layers are meant to provide faster mine-laying capability in challenging areas.The Advanced Light Helicopters will be used by the Army and Air Force for missions across different terrains and operational situations.Trawl Tanks and the Sarvatra Bridge System will be used to provide crossings for fighting formations during operations in different terrains.Navy gets radar and marine gas turbine approvalsFor the Indian Navy, the DAC cleared the procurement of Arudhra Radars and the design and development, followed by procurement, of Marine Gas Turbines.The Arudhra Radars will replace existing Air Route Surveillance Radars at various Naval Air Stations.Marine Gas Turbines are used for warship propulsion. Their design and development in India is intended to reduce the Navy's dependence on foreign vendors.Air Force proposals include jammers and secure access cardsFor the Indian Air Force, the council approved several proposals aimed at enhancing the capabilities of fighter aircraft, transport aircraft and helicopters.The DAC also cleared the procurement of Ground-Based Multi-Purpose Jammers and the installation of the Defence Forces Secure Access Card system.The jammers will be used against adversary radars, while the DEFSAC system will replace existing paper-based identity cards, passes and permits with interoperable smart cards using radio-frequency identification technology.An Acceptance of Necessity is an in-principle administrative approval that allows a procurement proposal to move forward in the defence acquisition process. It does not by itself amount to the signing of a procurement contract.

articles.title: Iran and Ukraine wars: Why ship fuel is running short, and why it matters
articles.summary: There’s less crude in the market, and refiners prefer to produce diesel. The result: Ships are running short of fuel.
articles.body:
The shipping industry, already heavily constrained by restrictions on transit through key waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz, faces another challenge stemming from the US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine: a shortage of fuel oil used by ships and power plants.

The fuel used by ships powers the transport of large cargoes around the world. Any shortage of this fuel could drive up global freight costs, which could in turn affect consumers and manufacturers of goods and commodities.

Most ships and oil tankers mainly use heavy fuel oil (HFO), commonly known as bunker fuel, to power their engines. This fuel is produced when crude oil is refined.

Other commonly used marine fuels include marine gas oil (used by smaller vessels), marine diesel oil (used in marine engines) and less polluting fuels like very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO).

Why is ship fuel running low and why does it matter?

According to analysts, the wars in West Asia and Europe, along with refiners opting to produce more profitable fuels, have contributed to the shortage.

Middle East fuel oil exports were down by 45 percent year on year to an average of 447,000 barrels per day from March to August, data from energy trade analytics firm Kpler shows.

Energy consultancy Energy Aspects told Reuters news agency that it expects the fuel oil market to face a deficit of 218,000 bpd in the third quarter. This is the first shortfall it has estimated since the third quarter of 2025, when it was a marginal 6,000 bpd.

How have wars in West Asia and the Russia-Ukraine war impacted fuel oil?

The US-Israel war on Iran has paralysed key maritime trade routes like the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20 percent of global oil and gas passed before the start of the war.

Iran has also hit multiple oil facilities in the Gulf in retaliation against the US.

Attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on shipping in the Red Sea and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes, have also disrupted shipping and constrained supply routes.

Royston Huan, a senior oil products analyst at analytics firm Energy Aspects told Al Jazeera that since April, the company has noticed a 400,000 bpd reduction in ship fuel sales compared to levels a year-ago — which were 6.9 million bpd. Over a year, that would translate to an average of 2 million tonnes of fuel oil less every month

“For perspective, this supply loss is about the same magnitude as all of China’s bunker sales volume,” Huan explained. China is a major oil refiner.

Besides the war on Iran, Russia’s ongoing war on Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies. Ukraine has in recent weeks bombed multiple major Russian refineries.

Russia is the world’s second-largest exporter of crude oil. Ukrainian drone attacks have affected Russia’s refinery output, with its fuel oil exports in August hitting a record low 591,000 bpd, down from an average of over 860,000 bpd in 2025, according to Kpler data going ⁠back to 2017.

The net result: less crude is being shipped out from key oil-producing regions, especially the Gulf and Russia.

That has meant an overall shortage in supplies of crude. And oil companies aren’t prioritising fuel oil as their product of choice.

What are refiners prioritising with the crude oil they’re getting?

Petrol, diesel and jet fuel, which are also produced when crude oil is refined, have all been impacted. But products like diesel tend to help suppliers generate higher profits, and they prioritise it over products like fuel oil.

According to Kpler, Nigeria’s 650,000-bpd Dangote refinery, for instance, has ramped up diesel, petrol and jet fuel exports, while its fuel oil exports have dropped.

Market observer Sunil Reddy said in a post on X on Monday that one of the key reasons for a global ship-fuel shortage is “the extraordinary profitability of diesel”.

“When diesel cracks [or] spreads become extremely high, refiners have a powerful incentive to squeeze as much diesel and [petrol] as possible out of every barrel. That changes what happens to the heavier part of crude,” he said.

He explained that in the refining process, instead of “allowing more of that heavy [oil] residue to remain as fuel oil for ships, refiners will send it through secondary processing units and upgrade it into higher-value products such as diesel”.

“So, extremely strong diesel margins effectively start pulling barrels away from the bunker-fuel market,” he said, adding that this would increase ship-fuel prices as well.

While a drop in ship fuel will have a large-scale impact on global shipping, Asia could be particularly affected because of its dependence on the Gulf.

According to Kpler data, Singapore, the world’s largest bunker hub, imports more than half of the nearly one million ⁠bpd of fuel oil it consumes. A drop in fuel oil supplies has also led to a rise in the price of shipping fuels like VLSFO.

In Singapore, the price of this fuel is up 76 percent since the war on Iran began to just less than $825 per metric tonne, or $130 a barrel, as of September 1, according to data ⁠from bunker price platform ZeroNorth.

Besides Singapore, fuel oil stocks in Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp in the Netherlands and Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates are also about 30 percent below their three-year seasonal averages, according to Reuters.

Market observer Reddy said on X: “The world economy is built on thousands of interdependent supply chains. One product depends on another country for raw materials, another for processing, another for machinery, another for energy.”

“Without ships, globalisation breaks. When ship fuel becomes too scarce or too expensive, many things don’t just become more expensive,” he added.

“At some point, some trade simply stops making economic sense.”

Huan from Energy Aspects said that a fall in ship fuel production raises its cost if the demand for the fuel hasn’t changed.

“Ship fuels (bunker fuels) are significant costs on voyages, which in turn tend to be passed on to the end user. The end user usually ends up bearing these higher costs, not so much the vessel owner,” he added.

Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at the United Kingdom-based firm Capital Economics, agreed. He told Al Jazeera that the lack of fuel oil supply is putting significant upward pressure on prices, which could contribute to higher shipping costs.

“Given the lack of spare refining capacity globally, prices are likely to remain high until there is a resolution to the conflict in the Middle East,” he added.

articles.title: Wild ferrets in Guernsey the focus of year-long research project
articles.summary: A conservation group has been spending a year studying wild ferrets after securing government funds.
articles.body:
The results of a year-long research project are expected to reveal more about Guernsey's wild ferret population than ever, project leaders have said.

Using money from the government's Strategy for Nature fund, La Société Guernesiaise has been tracking the animals by using specialist camera equipment.

The conservation charity said it plotted where devices should be located in areas where ferrets had been known to attack different wildlife, such as La Claire Mare Nature Reserve in St Peters, had taken thousands of photos and the pictures were now being examined.

La Société said it had been aware of the feral ferret population for some time, but "didn't know anything about them".

The charity was one of 11 local projects to be given funding from the Strategy for Nature last year , and applied for cash to buy 15 camera traps.

The traps were motion-activated and used to take photos or videos of wildlife and people without anyone having to be there to operate them, project leaders said.

Leah Cottell, who has been leading the study, said the process had been "incredibly time-consuming" but she had learned a lot.

"I knew that we had ferrets on the island, but we didn't really know anything about them," she told BBC Guernsey.

"They seem to like being around water sites because they like eating things like eggs, and so they'll go for the nests of ground-nesting birds."

However, despite the numbers, ferrets were not native to Guernsey, she added.

"They are an invasive species, and the feeling is that it's probably due to releases from domestic ferrets.

"They look like their polecat wild counterparts, so they have been out there for a very long time; or ferret owners in the 1980s might have let some go and over time it's expanded."

Cottell added it would take "months and months" to sift through all the photos, but the charity would write up a report of its findings.

The next round of Strategy for Nature funding is open, and people wishing to apply for money had until 25 October, fund bosses said.

articles.title: Ukraine's front lines are so dangerous that troops take casualties just moving in and out of their own trenches
articles.summary: Ukraine's drone-filled front lines have made even routine movement in and out of trenches a deadly risk for troops.
articles.body:
Ukrainian troops often take casualties moving in and out of trenches, a Western commander said.

Drones and other weapons make even routine movement near the front extremely dangerous.

The threat can leave soldiers stuck in defensive positions for days or even longer.

Ukraine's front lines are unforgivingly brutal, and soldiers are often injured or killed just rotating in and out of their own trench systems, a Western commander leading a training program for Ukrainian soldiers told Business Insider.

"We hear that Ukrainian forces take quite a few casualties infiltrating and exfiltrating out of their own trench systems because the front has been static for a very long time," said Brigadier Atle Molde, the commander of Task Force Legio, a Norway-led multinational effort to train Ukrainian soldiers on NATO soil.

Swarms of drones overhead gather intelligence and attack, making any movement a risk. Ukrainian commanders have described troop rotations as among the most vulnerable moments for front-line soldiers.

The drone-saturated area around the front lines is often described as a "kill zone. " A Ukrainian official previously told Business Insider that just getting to front-line positions can take days and that it is the most dangerous part of the mission in many cases.

Troop rotation, resupply, and relocation also present tremendous risks.

That danger is why the Western training program puts particular emphasis on moving in and out of trench systems. At Camp Jomsborg, a purpose-built training site in eastern Poland, "it's all about saving lives," Molde said.

Jørgen, a Norwegian Army instructor for the operation's platoon leader course who spoke on the condition that only his first name be used, told Business Insider that the training includes using supporting fire to suppress the enemy so that friendly forces can move into trenches.

He said that many of the Ukrainians who come through already have an "incredibly high" level of combat experience and have developed effective methods of their own. The input he has received from Ukrainian trainees "worked when I actually tried to do it," he shared, and resulted in "less risk to our guys."

Death and danger around defensive fighting positions

Trenches have long been surrounded by death and difficulty in this war. Worsening threats, particularly the drone threat, however, have at times made this situation significantly more dangerous.

Soldiers can get stuck inside trenches, dugouts, and other defensive positions for long periods.

Some troops have described having to spend months in a single position because drones and artillery made it too dangerous to move out safely. They had to wait for weather, friendly fire support, or a lucky break to move without immediately being detected and attacked.

A US veteran who fought for Ukraine previously told Business Insider that life in a trench was often just waiting as "artillery shells just dropping on you for hours on end," they said.

The danger can make seemingly basic tasks difficult. The veteran said troops couldn't even properly remove enemy dead, while another American vet who fought for Ukraine said that soldiers sometimes struggled to deepen or fortify their trenches because they didn't want to "stick their heads out."

"When guys have tried to move," the veteran said, "they step out and immediately just start getting pounded, and then they're having to play dead, hoping that eventually they'll catch a quick break to get up and start running."

Even staying put can offer little security. They described being "literally just hunkered down" and hoping nothing collapsed the position or landed inside the trench. "You're static in one spot, and there's not much you can do about it."

When troops can't safely rotate in and out, soldiers can end up stranded at the front for long periods.

Soldiers from Ukraine's 121st Territorial Brigade said in August that they had gone four months without a rotation and were running short of food and water, the Kyiv Independent reported at the time.

Command said that they would be pulled out when the security situation allowed. Heavy drone surveillance had made movement to and from forward positions difficult.

At Camp Jomsborg, Ukrainian combat experience, including its deep knowledge of trench warfare, is being combined with Western best practices and incorporated into how troops train to move through and fight from trenches.

Jørgen said the trench infiltration and exfiltration tactics the Ukrainians had shown him were better than any single lesson he had to offer. "Keeping it to the principles and trying to let the guys put their own experience into it," he said, "I think that's much more valuable than my experience."

The trench warfare in Ukraine is unlike anything Western militaries have seen in a long time. Positions are watched by drones, the battlefield kill chains are faster, allowing movement to be detected and engaged in minutes, and even routine supply runs and rotations can become deadly combat operations.

The West is paying attention and, through work with the Ukrainians, reassessing its training and assumptions about this kind of warfighting.

At Camp Jomsborg, leaders are trying to get the trenches to resemble those that Ukrainian troops actually encounter. The training trenches are "constructed by the Ukrainians, or they have told us how to construct it" to resemble the real ones as much as possible, Molde said.

He said the trench network has been "changed a couple of times already, and we've only been active for less than a year," highlighting the challenge of keeping up with a fast-evolving battlefield.

Though less of a focus for many Western militaries, trench operations are a critical and deadly part of regular operations, so it's a priority at Jomsborg. He said the goal is for as many Ukrainians to " survive this fight for as long as possible."

The hope, he added, is that "we reach a situation where Ukraine can negotiate a truce or a ceasefire on good terms. That's what it's all about."

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Can Iran enforce a restricted zone in the Strait of Hormuz?
articles.summary: Iran unveils plans for a restricted zone, but will Tehran be able to enforce it amid escalating tensions with the US?
articles.body:
Iran says it plans to establish a new restricted zone around the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, after Tehran and Washington traded attacks on ships in the crucial waterway in what experts called a “dangerous escalation”.

The two sides have been engaged in on-and-off attacks since a 60-day memorandum of understanding (MoU), signed on June 17, expired last month.

The latest escalation started after Iran targeted US warships patrolling and escorting oil tankers trying to evade the Tehran-imposed blockade of the strait. Meanwhile, a US naval blockade of the Iranian ports has drastically restricted its oil and other trade.

The MoU, which had ended the months-long military hostility, collapsed after 60 days due to disputes over who had ultimate control over the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has used as leverage in the war against the United States.

Oil tankers have become the latest targets in the US-Israel war on Iran, with Tehran repeatedly warning vessels against using unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz amid reports that a growing number of oil tankers are passing through the waterway. Prior to the start of the war, 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies flowed through the strait.

So, where exactly will Iran’s proposed zone be, what restrictions will apply, and how does Tehran intend to enforce this?

What did Iran say about the restrictive zone?

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said the zone would be announced in the coming days.

“This zone will start from the US Navy’s blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf,” he said, according to Iranian state media. “Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list [of Iran].”

Rezaei said the zone would “begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf”.

However, Tehran has provided few details about the zone’s precise boundaries or what being placed on its sanctions list would mean for vessels entering it.

Rezaei said new maps detailing routes, worked on in conjunction with Oman for the Hormuz Strait, would also be approved soon.

“The maps of a new international corridor which lies in Iranian and Omani waters and in which Iran will have management have been agreed and should be signed in the coming days,” he added.

“We will only commit to the Strait of Hormuz being open when they [the Americans] stop the sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran.”

The announcement comes after Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said late last month that Iran and Oman had agreed on a temporary maritime route for ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, whose entry “would be through our territorial waters, and part of the exit route would also be through our territorial waters”.

There has been no immediate US or wider international response specifically to Rezaei’s announcement of the new zone.

However, on Sunday, Washington rejected an Iranian claim reported in local media that a US vessel had attempted to enter an area Tehran considers restricted and was attacked.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Captain Tim Hawkins called the Iranian account “a total lie”.

The alleged attack comes days after Washington targeted three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hit tankers and fired a ballistic missile towards US warships patrolling near the Strait of Hormuz.

Doesn’t Iran already prescribe a route for ships through Hormuz?

Yes. Iran is already demanding that vessels use routes it approves through the strait.

Iran first published a map of its approved navigation routes in April, directing vessels much closer to the Iranian coastline than they travelled before the war. The route currently authorised by it follows a corridor along Iran’s coast.

But Iran’s attempt to control navigation has been challenged by a separate route closer to Oman.

In June, Oman, working with the International Maritime Organization (IMO), a United Nations agency that oversees shipping at sea, laid out a southern corridor intended to restore safe navigation through the strait.

A Liberian-flagged tanker, the Stoic Warrior, subsequently used a route that took it close to the coasts of the United Arab Emirates and Oman before passing around the Musandam Peninsula, an Omani exclave.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) objected to it, declaring that “the only authorised route” was the one announced by Iran and warning that vessels crossing without its permission would be “unacceptable and extremely dangerous”.

Following the 14-point MoU signed in June in the Swiss city of Geneva, traffic in the strait had picked up. But the resumption of attacks has severely limited commercial shipping in and around the key waterway.

Under the MoU, the US agreed to end its naval blockade within 30 days, while Iran pledged to clear mines from the Strait of Hormuz and allow ships to pass “with no charge” for 60 days.

What is the current status of traffic in the Strait of Hormuz?

Traffic is still getting through, but at substantially reduced levels.

Before the conflict, about 20 million barrels of crude oil per day flowed through the waterway. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, speaking to media on Sunday, said current transits were averaging more than nine million barrels of oil per day.

When pipelines bypassing the strait are included, Wright said flows were probably at “two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows”.

“So Iranians are still causing trouble, but the United States Navy is winning that battle,” he said.

Bolstering US claims was the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre, which on Sunday said 59 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz in the previous 48 hours.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the waterway is under Washington’s control despite near-daily Iranian attacks on ships, going so far as to suggest renaming the Strait of Hormuz after himself.

Iran has disputed claims of growing traffic, claiming its chokehold on the waterway continues.

However, recent data from other maritime tracking companies and websites paints a mixed picture. Figures show only six vessels crossed the strait on Wednesday, 11 on Tuesday and five last Monday, with a 10-day average of just 13 vessels per day.

On Monday, marine analytics firm Kpler showed that an average of 10 commodity ships transited the strait per ⁠⁠day over the past 10 days, the lowest since May.

Before the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, more than 130 ships passed daily through the strait, which allowed free navigation. Now, the Trump administration is negotiating with Iran to open the strait.

Meanwhile, Iran’s nuclear programme, which Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu invoked to launch the war, has vanished from the headlines.

Tehran has so far demonstrated an ability to make passage through Hormuz dangerous, forcing ships to avoid the waterway. At least 19 seafarers have been killed and dozens of ships attacked since March.

Whether it can militarily enforce the much broader zone Rezaei has proposed – particularly against vessels protected by the US military – remains to be seen.

Stephen Zunes, founding chair of Middle Eastern Studies at the University of San Francisco, says Iran will struggle to enforce a restricted zone near the Strait of Hormuz.

“It’s hard to see how they will really be able to enforce it. Iranian ships and planes trying to enforce that would be very vulnerable to US attacks,” he told Al Jazeera. “But perhaps they are giving a warning, given there still would be some risk for shipping companies to not count on being able to get through the strait without suffering consequences.”

Zunes said Iran may be hoping to provoke a broader US military response, which could benefit Tehran politically by “justifying attacks” on neighbouring Gulf countries and US military facilities in the region.

That, in turn, could help Iran, as public opinion in the US seems against continuing the conflict, while pushing the Iranian public to “rally around the flag” amid growing economic hardship at home.

Moreover, Zunes noted, Iran’s plan for a restricted zone could be linked to its pending deal with Oman on shipping routes through the waterway.

If the deal with Oman is workable and something the US can accept, Iran could “pull back” from enforcing the restricted zone, Zunes said.

If not, then Tehran has “something ready to try to make it more problematic for Washington” to refuse the deal with Oman.

articles.title: Public consultation launched on plans for new Welsh renewable energy company
articles.summary: The proposed plans aim to reduce the cost of energy in the long-term, but won't be able to set bills.
articles.body:
People across the country are being asked to have their say on proposals for a new renewable energy company owned by the Welsh government.

It would "develop and own" wind and solar plants, and support local communities to take an ownership stake.

The Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government hope it can reduce the cost of bills in the long term, but the company would not directly set energy prices.

It does not set out to replace the organisations that provide energy direct to customers, with the government inviting people for views on how it should operate.

The plans were criticised by the Welsh Conservatives.

The Welsh government already owns a renewable onshore wind and solar developer - Trydan Gwyrdd Cymru (TGC).

Ministers in Cardiff are proposing to bring TGC together with other existing Welsh energy schemes, such as Ynni Cymru, which aims to expand locally-owned renewables and the government's energy service.

Enterprise Minister Adam Price told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast the government wanted an energy system that was "clean, cheap and owned by us".

Plug-in solar panels are coming to a shop near you - here's what to know

'Secret' underground energy could heat every home in capital city

The company would not "replace existing energy suppliers or directly set household electricity prices", it said in a consultation document.

It added that its purpose would be to "help Wales reduce energy costs over time by developing and owning renewable energy assets" and "supporting local and community ownership, investing in smart local energy systems".

It would also "help more organisations use locally generated energy" and try to attract investment into Welsh energy infrastructure.

The company would be separate from Great British Energy , which the UK government set up in 2024.

TGC is working on a number of projects on land owned by the Welsh government, including proposed wind farms at Carreg Wen near Aberdare and Glyn Cothi in Carmarthenshire.

The consultation asks if TGC should form the basis of the new company and whether it should use its name or call itself Ynni Cymru .

It also proposes that the company could take stakes in larger schemes - suggesting this could involve offshore wind, marine energy and nuclear.

The consultation looks at establishing a Welsh Energy Wealth Fund to allow energy projects "to support the most vulnerable in Wales as well as those living in areas where projects are being delivered".

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast , Price said: "Our vision for the future of the energy system in Wales is one in which it's clean, it's cheap and it's owned by us."

He said the organisation was bringing the different elements together "to create a single company that, if you like, has the range of expertise and the sort of critical mass of resources and knowledge to make a real difference".

Price said Wales was "an energy giant at the Industrial Revolution with coal, but unfortunately we didn't see the benefit of that being derived largely by our own people".

He added: "We don't want to make the same mistake with the huge potential that Wales has in this new energy revolution with renewable energy."

The minister said many of the levers for energy are decided at a UK level, but added that energy produced by a public energy company could allow "lower energy prices" through agreements with local large energy users.

During the 2026 election campaign Plaid Cymru promised that renewable energy projects would need to offer local communities a part of their profits if they were approved by a Plaid-led Welsh government.

The party had been criticised by Labour for "repeatedly" opposing green energy infrastructure for Wales, such as pylons.

Plaid had said it would establish a "strong presumption in favour of undergrounding", and the "use of wooden poles where necessary".

Janet Finch-Saunders, Welsh Conservative energy spokesperson, said: "While thousands of well-paid manufacturing jobs are being lost, the Welsh government's answer is another state-owned company and yet more wind turbines and solar farms across the Welsh countryside.

"Wales needs cheap, reliable energy to keep factories open, businesses competitive and household bills down."
