articles.title: DOJ’s civil rights unit tasked with voter fraud and 5 dead after cargo plane crashes in Miami: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Federal election monitors traditionally focused on protecting voter rights are tapped to tackle fraud.
articles.body: Federal election monitors traditionally focused on protecting voter rights are tapped to tackle fraud. Police arrest an armed man suspected of lunging at an Ohio gubernatorial candidate. And five people are dead after an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashes at Miami’s main airport. Here’s what to know today. DOJ civil rights unit retooled to focus on voter fraud The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has for decades sent election monitors to polling sites to protect voters from discrimination based on race, disability or language. Now, the Trump administration is giving it a new focus: voter fraud. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Harmeet Dhillon, a Republican who co-chaired Lawyers for Trump during the 2020 election, helms the division. She emailed employees asking them to serve among the 1,000 monitors she wants in place for the midterms, a person familiar with the matter said. The division has solicited staff lawyers to serve as monitors before. But the number nationwide has never reached 1,000 and it’s unusual for fraud to be on the agenda. Many employees have also been replaced by conservative hires, some of whom back the president’s false claim that he won in 2020. NBC News spoke with a half-dozen Justice Department veterans. Some worry the monitors could be used to help undermine confidence in elections if Trump is unhappy with the results. More about the concerns. Related news: Exclusive: As Trump pushes for data centers, voters in key midterm races say they don’t want them. Poll: Most Americans are using AI, but they’re not happy about it. Alarm in Europe after far-right’s historic German victory A regional election victory put the far-right on the brink of holding power in a German state for the first time since the Nazis. The Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, crushed its mainstream rivals but fell just short of a majority in the eastern Saxony-Anhalt region. The pro-Russia, anti-immigration AfD is now seeking outside support in its bid to become the first far-right party to govern a state since World War II. As those high-stakes talks began, the shockwaves of Sunday’s vote were being felt across the continent. “It clearly sends out a very, very worrying signal,” French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told RTL ​radio, according to Reuters. “This shows that we face a ​major challenge in the face of a populist wave ‌which ⁠is spreading around the world today and which we must resist,” he said. In Poland, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also said the regional election was “a very worrying sign,” according to Reuters. “Only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD,” Poland’s center-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Suspect arrested after armed man confronts Ohio gubernatorial candidate A suspect was arrested after an armed man lunged at Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, and injured several people at a fair. Acton was speaking at the event when Patrick Havas, 38, “started pushing his way through the crowd,” a spokesperson for the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office said. Security confronted him, and two people were knocked to the ground in the process. After law enforcement officials arrested Havas, they recovered two handguns and a set of brass knuckles, the spokesperson added. Acton, a physician, was not hurt, and she remained on-site to attend to one of the injured people, according to a photo an attendee shared with NBC News. Here’s what else we know. Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes in Miami Five people were killed and five others injured after an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashed just outside Miami International Airport yesterday, officials said. The Boeing 767-300 aircraft overran the runway while it was landing, struck multiple vehicles and came to rest at a field, according to officials. It took off from San Juan, Puerto Rico, the Federal Aviation Administration said. Three people were in critical condition, the Miami-Dade fire chief said. A hotline has been set up for relatives of people who may have been involved in the accident. Read the full story here. NBC Selected: Shop 150+ Labor Day sales before they’re gone for good Today is your last opportunity to save big on major brands before Black Friday. You can shop Shark, Brooks, Stanley, Kiehl’s and more for as little as $12 on Amazon, and snag up to 75% off at Target, Old Navy, Home Depot, Ulta and more. See the full list of Labor Day deals here. Sign up to The Selection newsletter for hands-on product reviews, expert shopping tips and a look at the best deals and sales each week. Staff Pick: The U.K.’s approach to postpartum psychosis may be saving lives Lindsay Clancy’s devastating trial over the killing of her three children has sparked an important dialogue around maternal mental healthcare and how cases of postpartum psychosis are treated in the U.S. We looked at an approach across the Atlantic that prioritizes the treatment of mothers alongside their babies through specialist inpatient care facilities called Mother and Baby Units, or MBUs. While the United Kingdom is not the only country to provide care that keeps mothers and babies together during treatment, the scale of its MBU program is “pretty unique to the U.K.,” Dr. Sally Wilson, the National Training Coordinator for Action on Postpartum Psychosis, a British charity supporting women and families affected by the condition, told me. My reporting highlights how that trailblazing effort may very well be saving lives, including that of one mom, Sofii Lewis, who says she and her daughter Evie, now 3, might not be alive today had it not been for the care she received in an MBU. — Chantal Da Silva, world news reporter Read All About It At the early Emmys, “Widow’s Bay” took home eight awards, “The Pitt” snagged four and Rob Reiner posthumously won the best guest actor in a comedy category for his work on “The Bear.” Reiner’s friend and fellow “Bear” guest star Jamie Lee Curtis was among those in the crowd paying him tribute.Israel’s air force carried out two airstrikes on a southern Lebanese village early this morning, killing at least nine people and wounding others, including women and children, Lebanon’s Health Ministry said. Andrew Williams, the guitarist for metalcore band Every Time I Die, who went by “The Butcher” in his other career as a professional wrestler, died at 48. A fireworks explosion at a festival in Mexico killed at least 10 people and injured more than 60. Thanks for reading today’s Morning Rundown. Today’s newsletter was curated for you by Kayla Hayempour and David Hickey. If you’re a fan, please send a link to your family and friends. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Iran to announce ‘restricted zone’ near Strait of Hormuz as tensions simmer
articles.summary: Iran is set to announce a “restricted zone” close to the Strait of Hormuz following recent exchanges of fire between the U.S. and the Middle Eastern country. According to a Sunday report by Press TV, an Iranian state media outlet, a new restricted zone was set to be declared near the strait within the next…
articles.body:
Iran is set to announce a “restricted zone” close to the Strait of Hormuz following recent exchanges of fire between the U.S. and the Middle Eastern country.

According to a Sunday report by Press TV , an Iranian state media outlet, a new restricted zone was set to be declared near the strait within the next few days, Iran’s top security official said. All vessels coming into the zone that are not cooperating with the Iranians will be put on a sanctions list.

Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Major Gen. Mohsen Rezaei said Sunday night on television that the zone “will begin from the US Navy’s blockade line and extend into parts of the Persian Gulf,” per Press TV.

The Iran war just stretched past the six-month mark, with the conflict straining U.S. relations with historic allies, driving up oil and gas prices amid the Strait of Hormuz’s closure and proving unpopular with the American public in recent polling.

Press TV also reported Sunday that Iran said that it had attacked an American ship in the strait . A U.S. military vessel, which was remotely-operated, was attacked by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), per the military group.

According to a statement from the IRGC, the vessel had been trying to go into a restricted portion of the strait, Press TV reported.

“With the grace and favor of Almighty God, every desperate move by the enemy is being closely monitored by brave, self-sacrificing IRGC Navy forces and will be met with a decisive attack,” the IRGC said in its Sunday statement, per Press TV.

The attack was carried out in retaliation for the U.S. military conducting strikes against multiple Iranian crude oil carriers because of “multiple unprovoked” attacks from Iran on two American warships, U.S. Central Command said.

articles.title: The poorest in the U.S. can’t find housing even as low-income units sit empty
articles.summary: Mathew Davis, who lives in a homeless shelter in Austin, Texas, would love an apartment of his own.
articles.body: PORTLAND, Ore. — Mathew Davis, who lives in a homeless shelter in Austin, Texas, would love an apartment of his own. But with the little money he makes donating blood plasma, even a $450-a-month tiny home with no running water and a communal bathroom would be a stretch. Meanwhile, over 4,500 units the city classifies as affordable — nearly 16% — sit empty. “I don’t make enough money really to afford anything,” Davis, 49, said of the few hundred dollars he earns a month. “I just keep trying to swim uphill.” The poorest people in the U.S. face the most acute shortages of affordable homes. But the majority of low-income housing financed in recent years is for those earning 50% of an area’s median income or above, according to a survey of state housing agencies. Some cities are now seeing an uptick in vacancies as rents for these units approach market rates. The result: Apartments designated as affordable sit empty because the poorest of the poor cannot afford them. Meanwhile, some people are forced into homelessness and others into desperate circumstances to pay for housing they can’t afford. The poorest have few housing options There are only about 4 million affordable rental units available for the country’s 11 million extremely low-income renter households, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition’s most recent annual report. These are people with annual incomes either below the federal poverty guidelines — just under $16,000 for a single-person household — or 30% of the median income in their area, whichever is higher. They comprise about a quarter of U.S. renter households, and include many people working low-wage jobs, seniors and those with disabilities living on fixed incomes. About three-quarters of extremely low-income renter households pay over half their income on rent and utilities, the report said, leaving little leftover for other necessities. Yet homes set aside for these renters were only about 12% of the affordable housing units financed in 2024 by the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit — a federal program providing tax credits to developers in exchange for keeping rents low for at least 30 years, according to figures from the National Council of State Housing Agencies. The majority are for those earning at least 50% of an area’s median income, or AMI. In Austin, that’s a single person earning roughly $47,000 a year, as compared with an extremely low-income person earning under $28,000. The program has financed nearly 4 million affordable units nationwide since its creation 40 years ago. But some experts say it’s inefficient — and more costly than housing vouchers. “It’s enormously complex and bureaucratic, and it raises the cost of construction enormously because the rules are so complicated,” said Chris Edwards, an economist at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, who told Congress the program’s complexity “spawned” an industry of law and accounting firms just to administer it. “If you’re going to subsidize affordable housing, you should give the money directly to tenants,” he said, referring to housing vouchers. Other experts say the two programs work together well because properties built with the tax credit are required to accept vouchers — while landlords of market-rate apartments in many states are not. Still, there’s a major federal funding shortfall: Experts estimate only one-in-four eligible families ever receive vouchers. Vouchers can help the poorest pay for housing that’s targeted to higher income groups, but the waitlist can be yearslong. Some affordable housing developers say that without vouchers, it’s not economically feasible to provide units for extremely low-income people. True Ground Housing Partners, an affordable housing developer in the Washington, D.C., area, gives an example: A unit for those earning 60% of the area’s median income — nearly $70,000 a year — brings in $1,715 per month in rent. But after $1,575 in mortgage and operating expenses, only $140 is left. “The math does not lie,” said president and CEO Carmen Romero, noting that an extremely low-income person would pay only half that rent. “Our expenses don’t make it really possible to create a 30% AMI unit, unless there was this extraordinary amount of subsidy that just doesn’t exist.” Affordable housing competes with market-rate rents Meanwhile, affordable housing rents for 60% AMI units are approaching those of market-rate apartments in U.S. cities like Austin, Denver and Portland, Oregon. As a result, some people are opting to pay a bit more for market-rate apartments with less income-verification and faster approval — leaving growing numbers of affordable units vacant. In Austin, the vacancy rate for all affordable housing is nearly 16% with over 4,500 vacant units, according to real estate data and analytics firm CoStar. A healthy vacancy rate is around 5%. LDG Development, an affordable housing developer, cited a 12% vacancy rate for its 60% AMI units in Austin. Chief portfolio officer Rebekah Fischer said LDG is “in direct competition” with the thousands of new market-rate apartments recently built in Austin. “I have to have every bank statement, every pay check, every bill, every Venmo transaction that you had with your friends,” Fischer said of affordable housing applicants. “When we’re almost going after the same renter, you can be approved within two minutes at a market-rate deal, where unfortunately in affordable housing … it takes time.” In Denver, there’s a 13% vacancy rate among 60% AMI units financed by the federal tax credit program — and a 21% vacancy rate for 80% AMI units, according to the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority. Meanwhile, there is far too little housing for the city’s poorest. In Portland, where there is also a housing shortage for the lowest income groups, there are over 1,700 vacant affordable units for an overall vacancy rate of 7.5%, according to the Portland Housing Bureau. Most are for those earning 60% AMI, or about $54,000 for a single-person household, with rent capped at $1,444 per month. That’s close to the average rent of $1,581 for a one-bedroom market-rate apartment, according to CoStar figures shared by the bureau. Portland resident Jaiden Barbee earns around 55% of the area median income and is on waitlists for affordable housing. But, he says, he’d pay more for a market-rate apartment to avoid the lengthy application process. “I’d rather spend the $200 extra just to get into a place easier that’s wherever I want” and doesn’t have “all these hoops,” he said. ‘I want to shut the door at night and sleep’ Austin officials set a goal of building 20,000 units between 2018 and 2027 for extremely low-income people — 17% of the city’s households. Just 543 were built as of 2024, city documents show. Meanwhile, all 15,000 units planned for those earning between 60% and 80% of area median income were built. In response to questions from The Associated Press, the Austin housing department said it recognized the need to do more to produce housing for the poorest people and was taking steps to do that, including giving preference to funding proposals that include 30% AMI units. For Davis, who lived in his car for a year before getting a bed in the Austin shelter, the housing shortage for people like him is frustrating. “I want to shut the door at night and be able to sleep,” he said. “I really just want to find the right place.”

articles.summary: Monday is the last day before Canada’s “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs are set to go into effect, two weeks after President Trump put 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian products. There have not been reports of renewed negotiations between the two countries. “Canada’s Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” Trump…
articles.body:
Monday is the last day before Canada’s “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs are set to go into effect, two weeks after President Trump put 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian products.

There have not been reports of renewed negotiations between the two countries.

“Canada’s Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday . “It has been that way for years — but no longer!”

The U.S. is simultaneously continuing to spar with Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, with both countries exchanging vessel strikes over the weekend. Meanwhile, service members on the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose extended deployment sparked controversy due to reports of poor conditions, are finally sailing home after a brief “recharge” in Thailand.

Big Tech is also facing some of its fiercest resistance yet from Americans finding rare common ground over the technology industry’s growing footprint across the country.

From protests over data centers and AI-powered surveillance cameras to landmark verdicts against social media platforms, backlash against Big Tech is reaching a fever pitch, in both political parties. Insiders can read more here .

The president on Monday set to return to Washington from his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., after the long weekend.
